newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Artists lobby EP on resale rights.
newsitem.headline: Artists lobby EP on resale rights.

text.p: Twenty thousand plastic and graphic artists, fearing they will lose out under impending European Union legislation on resale rights, have written to Euro-MPs ahead of a key parliamentary vote this week.

The European Parliament will this week vote on its first reading of the Commission's proposal for a directive on the resale right for the benefit of the author of an original work of art -- COM(96)97.
The artists grouped in the European Visual Artists and copyright organisation GESAC, are strongly in favour of the EU's move to harmonise the resale right throughout the EU.

Under the directive artists in every member state -- including Britain where they are currently denied this right -- would be entitled to a percentage of the price whenever one of their works was resold.

But the artists are alarmed by two provisions in the report of Spanish European People's Party deputy Ana Vallelersundi Palacio -- on thresholds and rates -- which would mean that artists in a number of member states which currently have a high level of protection would lose out.
Palacio recommends that the rights guaranteed by the directive should only apply to works of art that sold for at least 1,000 Ecus.

But the artists say that unless this threshold is lowered to 500 Ecus young artists at the start of their careers and lesser-known artists -- those who are struggling most to make out -- will miss out.
The artists are also alarmed that Palacio has reduced the tapering scale of rates which the artists concerned would receive whenever one of their works was resold.
Palacio has proposed giving artists four percent on sales valued at 1,000 to 50,000 ecus, three percent from 50,000 to 100,000 ecus and 1.5 percent above that.
The artists argue that this would produce "swingeing and wholly unwarranted cuts in the incomes they currently earn from the resale of their works in those member states which apply a single rate."

In France, for example, where a single rate of three percent currently applies, using the rates proposed in the Palacio report to a work sold for 250,000 Ecus would cut the artists' income by 23 percent.
"The loss of income on the same sale in Germany - which has a single rate of five percent - would be 54 percent," the artists' group said in a statement.

They said that they had already compromised in accepting the levels of five percent on sales worth 500 to 50,000 Ecus, three percent from 50,000 to 250,000 ecus and one percent above 250,000 ecus proposed by the parliament's Culture Committee.
"Below that level of protection the drop in their incomes would literally be such as to literally dispossess them of their legitimate rights," they said.
